This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.
video_title: Why your LED fades look wrong (1 line fix) #arduino #iot #led

text: Pretty much yeah. Gamma 2.2 is slightly steeper than a simple quadratic curve. The reason that specific number shows up everywhere is partly because human brightness perception is nonlinear, and partly because old CRT displays (the big chunky old TV screens) naturally had an approximately (x^2.2) brightness response. Modern image/video standards ended up standardising around compensating for that curve, and it also happens to map pretty well to how our eyes perceive brightness changes.

video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.

video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

video_description:
This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

text: Great question: You can, and averaging multiple gyros can reduce random noise. The catch is that drift is often caused by bias, not just random noise. If all the gyros are slightly wrong in a consistent way, averaging still leaves you with a biased value that gets integrated over time. So stacking gyros helps precision/redundancy, but you still usually need calibration or an external reference to fix long-term drift.

video_description:
This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

text:
Not necessarily, you can output a key press or release event as soon as you notice the first change, then you just ignore any other changes until the debounce period for that key has elapsed.

It may be an issue for games that require you to very quickly tap the same key multiple times. But I don't think there are too many such games and there are a few hardware options that let you fine tune firmware settings.

The one game that I know for sure people need to do that is NES/BPS aka "Classic" Tetris. But I don't even think it does debouncing, it just reads the controller once every frame and that's it. I've heard some drama over usage of certain keyboards between osu and trackmania players, but I haven't really paid attention to any of that.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

ai_draft_text: There can definitely be electrical ringing, especially with long wires or fast edges, but switch bounce is very much a real mechanical effect from the contacts making and breaking a few times before settling. For typical MCU button inputs, electron “inertia” is negligible compared with contact mechanics, input thresholds, pullups, and stray capacitance. Twisted pair and termination matter more once the wiring starts behaving like a transmission line.
text:
I dont think the button contacts physically bounce, it is the electrical current which "rings".
There are a lot of electromagnetic forces. The wire has a very tiny inductance/capacitance once current starts flowing. Theres also an astronomically small momentum for the flow of electrons in the wire which becomes apparent on very sensitive microcontrollers.

You can reduce the bounce with several methods that deal with the inductance and the inertia of electrons, some communications bus networks require them. You run the two wires feeding the wire in a twisted pair to cancel inductance. You can use resistors at both ends as a pull up and canceling pull down to supply a small current through the wires below the High-threshold of the microcontroller, having a small amount of current flow reduces the ringing or bouncing when the wire goes high.

text: Could you also do this in hardware? For example with a small capacitor?
video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.
video_title: Your Button Is Lying to Your Microcontroller...

text: You absolutely could! I presume you’re talking about an RC low-pass filter, which is the hardware way of solving the same problem. The resistor and capacitor smooth out the rapid voltage changes from the contact bounce before they ever reach the microcontroller. I just chose the software approach since it’s simple and doesn’t require any extra components.

text:
Back in the days, there were also push buttons with both NO and NC contacts. The NO contacts would trigger the Set pin of a an RS flipflop, the NC pin the Reset pin.

You can build two RS flipflops with the four NAND gates in an SN74LS00.

Nowadays it's cheaper to do it in software. We know that the switches inside a mechanical keyboard can bounce for  up to 5 ms (up to 10 ms for worn-out or low-quality switches), so we ignore every key for 5 - 10 milliseconds after it has been pressed or released. But that requires a lot of RAM (or registers) for a typical ~100 key keyboard. Well, "lots of RAM" means like two dozen bytes, maybe 60 bytes, or more depending on you scan speed. We're talking about extremely cheap microcontrollers here, like the AT90S1200!

Or you just use a polling rate which is longer than 10 ms.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.
video_title: Your Button Is Lying to Your Microcontroller...

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

video_description:
This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

text:
Thank you for the lovely question I’m really happy to see people so engaged! 

You CAN use multiple gyros, and high-end systems often do for redundancy/noise reduction. BUT (and it’s a big but) the tricky part is that if all the gyros have unknown bias, algebra alone can’t tell you which part is real rotation and which part is shared drift. Averaging can reduce random noise, but constant bias still gets integrated into orientation error. To actually correct drift long-term you usually need an external reference, like gravity from an accelerometer, magnetic north from a magnetometer, GPS, vision, etc.

The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

text: For a sensor like this, being on the equator wouldn't make any noticeable difference. The drift shown in the video is dominated by sensor bias and integration error, not Earth's rotation. Interestingly, sufficiently accurate gyroscopes can detect Earth's rotation (~15°/hour), but an MPU6050 is nowhere near accurate enough for that effect to dominate the drift you're seeing here.

text: Great question! They drift too, just in different ways. The key is that the gyro measures a rate that must be integrated, so tiny biases accumulate indefinitely. Accelerometers and magnetometers provide absolute references (gravity and magnetic north), so while they're noisy and can be miscalibrated, their errors usually don't accumulate in the same runaway way. Sensor fusion works because the sensors have different failure modes and can help correct each other.

his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.

The missile knows where it is at all times. It knows this because it knows where it isn't. By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. The guidance subsystem uses deviations to generate corrective commands to drive the missile from a position where it is to a position where it isn't, and arriving at a position where it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the position where it is, is now the position that it wasn't, and it follows that the position that it was, is now the position that it isn't.
In the event that the position that it is in is not the position that it wasn't, the system has acquired a variation, the variation being the difference between where the missile is, and where it wasn't. If variation is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the GEA. However, the missile must also know where it was.
The missile guidance computer scenario works as follows. Because a variation has modified some of the information the missile has obtained, it is not sure just where it is. However, it is sure where it isn't, within reason, and it knows where it was. It now subtracts where it should be from where it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of where it shouldn't be, and where it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its variation, which is called error.

text: Actually curious why you couldn't build a ring of sensors to fire at the same time? You might end up with a slightly slower refresh rate at the expense of getting 360 sonar that shows everything around at the same moment. No moving machinery meaning it's easier to repair and maintain as well
video_title: This is NOT a RADAR. It's Sonar!  #arduino #electronics #engineering

text:
Great Question! There’s 2 main reasons:

1. For this specifically give that each sensor can only monitor a single degree you’d need a whopping 360 of these sensors, which is financially not the healthiest for your wallet and also pretty impractical space wise. 
2. The preferred approach (which I’m going to try out in the next few weeks) is to mount the sensor on a motor with a slip ring (removes the problem of cables getting tangled when spinning) and spin it around to get a full 360 degree picture of what you’re scanning. 

In practise I believe most industries prefer the second because it’s easier to maintain one sensor and one motor to spin it than it is to setup and configure 360 different sensors. Really love the thinking though!!

text:
Depends on the hardware and varies over time. AFAIK the default debounce period on QMK, a popular open source keyboard and mouse firmware, is 5ms.

As switches get worn with use, they'll start bouncing longer and longer than they used to when they were new. At some point, they'll start bouncing for longer than the debounce period of the firmware and you'll start having multiple clicks or keypresses for the worn switch.

You can usually get around 10 years of heavy use with decent hardware, after that, you may need to change worn switches. You can probably get away with just increasing the debounce period in your firmware if you're using a DIY keyboard or mouse, but I'd suggest you to just change the worn part.

You can usually find replacements for around a dollar each and it may last another decade or more of use. Think about it like a clutch or a CV joint in a car: they can last a long time, but not forever.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

text: Close, 1/2.2 is typically used for gamma encoding image/video data, whereas for perceptually smooth LED dimming we usually apply the curve in the other direction (x^2.2) because LEDs are roughly linear but human brightness perception isn’t. The terminology gets confusing because “gamma correction” can refer to either applying or removing gamma depending on the stage in the pipeline.

text: The drift is only around vertical axis, right ? Those méthods to correct drift is not enought for headset localisation for exemple
video_description:
This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

text: Pretty much yeah! Yaw/vertical-axis drift is usually the hardest to correct because gravity gives you a reference for roll/pitch via the accelerometer, but not for heading. And yeah, modern VR headsets go much further than simple IMU fusion: they also use cameras, SLAM, optical tracking, external markers/base stations, etc. Pure inertial tracking drifts too much on its own for accurate long-term headset localisation.

This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.

text:
Microswitches have a limited lifespan, but luckily, they're neither expensive nor hard to replace. Still, I'm a little pissed at Logitech as they started using switches with a far lower ratings than they used to.

I got a Logitech Marble Mouse in 2008 and it served me without hiccups for solid 10 years, until the left button microswitch got too bouncy for the hardcoded debounce delay of the firmware to filter out. I replaced the switch and gave that trackball to a friend, who still uses it with no issues to this day. Maybe he'll have to change that microswitch again in a few years, but IIRC I left a spare tucked inside the case for when that day comes.

I replaced it with a MX Ergo as I found it a lot nicer and I wanted to move from a index to a thumb trackball. It lasted 4 years before the rubberized finish started to flake out and get ridiculously gross. I ended up peeling the whole thing, it's ugly, but at least it isn't gross. Used it for another year until I got a Ploopy Thumb Trackball and I've been using it since then, for just over 3 years. I also have a M570 that I leave in my backpack as it's more compact and more practical to lug around than the Ploopy.

The same applies to keyboards, one of my friends had a key switch go bad after many years using the same keyboard, luckily he still had the accessories in storage and was able to find a few spare switches and a switch puller. It was hot swappable, so he didn't even had to bother with a soldering iron.

A 360° continuous rotation servo is definitely an option, but those control speed rather than position, so you'd have to estimate the angle based on time and rotation speed, which can drift over time.

video_description:
his video explains mechanical button bounce in microcontroller projects.

The video demonstrates a single button press being detected multiple times, then explains why: mechanical push buttons are not ideal switches. Inside the button, two metal contacts physically bounce against each other for a few milliseconds before settling, causing rapid on/off transitions. While these transitions are too fast for humans to notice, a microcontroller can easily detect them as multiple button presses.

The video then introduces debouncing as the solution, explaining that software can ignore additional transitions until the button has had time to settle, resulting in a single clean button press.

The tone is educational but approachable, focusing on the underlying physics rather than just the programming solution.

video_description: This video explains why LED fades driven by linearly increasing PWM values often look uneven to the human eye. Although the LED output changes linearly, human brightness perception is nonlinear—we're much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. Using simple graphs, the video compares a linear response, the eye's perception curve, and the inverse gamma correction curve, showing how remapping the PWM values with gamma correction produces a much smoother-looking fade. The implementation uses `pow(normalized, 2.2)` to clearly demonstrate the concept rather than the most optimized embedded implementation.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

video_description:
This video explains the fundamentals of PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control using a thrust-vector-controlled rocket as an intuitive example. The rocket's goal is to remain upright while external disturbances (such as wind) push it off course. The video first introduces Proportional (P) control, showing that the further the rocket tilts from its target orientation, the larger the corrective action becomes. It then demonstrates the downside of proportional control alone: the rocket overshoots and oscillates because it is still moving as it reaches the target.

The video next introduces Derivative (D) control, explaining that if the rocket is already rotating quickly back towards its target, the controller reduces the corrective action. This damps the motion and helps prevent overshoot and oscillation.

Finally, the video explains Integral (I) control using the example of a slightly weaker engine (or other constant disturbance). Proportional control alone leaves a small persistent error because it only reacts once an error exists. Integral control accumulates this persistent error over time and gradually adds a constant correction, eliminating the steady-state error so the rocket can remain perfectly on target. The explanation intentionally simplifies the mathematics in favour of intuition while remaining technically representative of how PID controllers behave in real engineering systems.

text: You CAN use multiple gyros, and high-end systems often do for redundancy/noise reduction. BUT (and it's a big but) the tricky part is that if all the gyros have unknown bias, algebra alone can't tell you which part is real rotation and which part is shared drift. Averaging can reduce random noise, but constant bias still gets integrated into orientation error. To actually correct drift long-term you usually need an external reference, like gravity from an accelerometer, magnetic north from a magnetometer, GPS, vision, etc.

video_description:
This video demonstrates gyroscope drift using an MPU6050 IMU connected to an ESP32 and a 3D cube visualization. The cube follows the sensor correctly while it is moving, but continues to slowly rotate even after the sensor is placed motionless on a table. The video explains that a MEMS gyroscope measures angular velocity using vibrating structures and Coriolis forces, and that orientation is obtained by integrating this angular velocity over time. Because even tiny sensor biases and noise are integrated continuously, the estimated orientation slowly drifts.

The video then introduces two common solutions: (1) calibration to estimate and subtract sensor bias, and (2) sensor fusion, where gyroscope data is combined with accelerometers (gravity reference) and magnetometers (heading reference) to continuously correct accumulated drift. The explanation is intentionally simplified for a broad audience while remaining technically accurate.
